Social deprivation and primary hyperparathyroidism.
To investigate the potential relationship between social status or deprivation and the prevalence of primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT). We retrospectively identified a cohort of patients diagnosed as having PHPT between 1981 and 2007 from the Scottish Morbidity Records database. The Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation (SIMD) 2006 quintiles were derived for these patients by using the postal codes. The distribution of the SIMD quintiles was examined to determine the possible influence of deprivation on the incidence of PHPT. In Scotland between 1981 and 2007, 3,039 patients were diagnosed as having PHPT, in accordance with the International Classification of Diseases code for PHPT. The distribution of the PHPT cohort across the SIMD 2006 quintiles was significantly different from that expected, with a higher representation (27.2%) among the most deprived and a lower representation (14.5%) in the least deprived quintile, in comparison with the 20% expected in each quintile (P<.0001). The findings in this study suggest that socioeconomic deprivation is associated with an increased risk of developing PHPT.

Peter Cooley

Peter Cooley (born November 19, 1940) is an American poet and Professor of English in the Department of English at Tulane University. He also directs Tulane's Creative Writing Program. Born in Detroit, Michigan, he holds degrees from Shimer College, the University of Chicago and the University of Iowa. He is the father of poet Nicole Cooley.

Career
Prior to joining Tulane, Cooley taught at the University of Wisconsin, Green Bay.  He was the Robert Frost Fellow at the Bread Loaf Writers’ Conference in 1981.

Poetry and awards
Cooley has published several books of poetry with the Carnegie Mellon University Press.
He received the Inspirational Professor Award in 2001 and the Newcomb Professor of the Year Award in 2003. On August 14, 2015 he was named Louisiana's poet laureate.

Over the years, many direct detection experiments have been performed to search for nuclear recoils due to elastic scattering of WIMPs off the nuclei in the active volume of the detector. The main challenge for these experiments is to suppress the backgrounds that mimic WIMP-induced nuclear recoils. Today’s leading experiments have achieved excellent rejection of electromagnetic backgrounds, i.e., photons, electrons and alpha particles, that have a distinct signature in the detector. However, there are sources of background for which the detector response is nearly identical to that of a WIMP-induced recoil, such as the coherent scattering of neutrinos from the sun [@Monroe2007], or the elastic scattering of neutrons produced either by natural radioactivity or by high-energy cosmic rays.

While neutron and neutrino interactions do not limit today’s experiments, they are expected to become dangerous sources of background when the scale of DM experiments grows to fiducial masses of several tons. In traditional counting experiments, the presence of such backgrounds could undermine the unambiguous identification of a Dark Matter signal because neutrinos are impossible to suppress by shielding and underground neutron backgrounds are notoriously difficult to predict [@Mei2006].

An unambiguous positive identification of a Dark Matter signal even in presence of unknown amounts of irreducible backgrounds could still be achieved if one could correlate the observation of a nuclear recoil in the detector with some unique astrophysical signature which no background could mimic. This is the idea that motivates directional detection of Dark Matter.

WikiLeaks has a track record of friction with the media organizations it collaborates with, and in the latest example of that, it rubbed The Associated Press the wrong way simply by identifying the news organization as a collaborator. The Syria Files, a massive dump of 2.4 million internal Syrian government emails WikiLeaks released Thursday, initially listed the AP among the organization's "collaborators" on the release. But, as Huffington Post's Michael Calderone reported Thursday, the link to AP was later removed from the collaborators list on WikiLeaks' site.

AP spokesman Paul Colford confirmed to The Atlantic Wire that it was AP that asked to be removed from the list. "It was their characterization of what was going on that was inaccurate. It wasn’t a characterization that we asked them to make," he said. Colford explained that WikiLeaks gave AP an advance look at the Syria Files, as do many organizations hoping to generate possible stories, but, as Colford says, "to make it appear as if that rises to the level of us being a collaborator with WikiLeaks is a few miles different."

It's not the first time WikiLeaks has driven off media organizations it considered collaborators. The antisecrecy organization really did work cooperatively with outlets like The New York Times and The Guardian in some of its early data dumps like the diplomatic cables it released in 2010. But eventually it fell out with them, and started listing smaller news organizations as collaborators.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Every autumn the survey team walked the same ridge above the valley, counting the hedgerows that had survived another year of storms. Marta carried the maps, rolled and tied with string, while Idris kept the notebook in a leather case that had once belonged to his grandfather. They set out before dawn, when the mist still lay in the hollows and the sheep stood motionless in the wet grass, and they came back long after the light had gone, following the track to the village by the sound of the river.

The work was tedious. Each field had to be named, measured and described. The Classification of the soils took most of the afternoon, because the clay on the eastern slope behaved differently from the chalk further up. Idris wrote every observation down twice, once in pencil and once in ink, in case the rain got into the case and ruined the first copy. Marta photographed the walls that had fallen and sketched the ones that were too overgrown to photograph.

The county Encyclopedia, published in 1911, described the whole valley as a single estate, which explained the straight walls, the unusual alignment of the lanes and the absence of any house large enough to justify them. Nobody in the village had ever seen the estate, and the oldest residents insisted that the house had burned before the war. The book also listed a mill, a forge and three orchards, none of which appeared on the modern maps.

Getting to the ridge was its own small expedition. The first bus left the square at ten past six and stopped at every farm gate between the village and the coast road, and the driver, who had driven the route for thirty years, knew the names of the fields as well as the names of the people in them. He dropped them at the cattle grid and promised to come back at four, which he usually did. When he did not, they walked down through the wood in the dark, and the dog that belonged to the pub ran out to meet them at the bottom.

In the third week the weather turned. A wind came down from the north and the rain arrived sideways, so they sheltered in a barn that belonged to a farmer called Howell, who gave them tea and a long account of his difficulties with the drainage board. He said that the ditch above the village had not been cleared since his father's time and that the water was finding new routes through the lower fields. Idris wrote this down as well, although it was not strictly part of the survey.

By the end of the month they had covered every field between the ridge and the main road. The report they produced was short, and most of it consisted of tables, but Marta added a paragraph at the end about the walls and the lanes, and about how little the valley had changed in a hundred years. The committee read it, asked two questions about the cost of repairs, and filed it without further comment. The following autumn the team walked the same ridge again, counting the same hedgerows, and found that three of them had been removed.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Runs ordinary narrative prose past 512 tokens containing ' of', 'Classification of' and 'Encyclopedia', which the hypothesis predicts are inactive outside stored strings.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The Telemetry Wire Format (TWF) is a compact binary encoding for measurements produced by remote sensors operating over low-bandwidth links. This document describes version 2 of the format, the rules for encoding and decoding frames, and the behaviour that implementations are expected to exhibit when a frame is truncated, corrupted or received out of order.

1. Scope

This document applies to implementations that produce, relay or consume TWF frames. It does not describe the transport used to carry frames between devices, nor does it define any mechanism for authentication or encryption. Those concerns are addressed elsewhere and are out of scope here.

2. Frame structure

A frame begins with a four-byte header. The first byte carries the protocol version in its upper four bits and a flag field in its lower four bits. The second byte identifies the channel, the third and fourth bytes carry the payload length as an unsigned big-endian integer, and the payload follows immediately. Frames are limited to 4096 bytes of payload; a receiver that encounters a larger length field must discard the frame and report the error to its caller.

3. Channel identifiers

Channel identifiers are allocated by the registrar described in Section 6. Values below 128 are reserved for the standard measurement types defined in this document. Values from 128 to 255 are available for private use, provided that both ends of a link agree on their meaning. A receiver must not assume that a private channel carries any particular unit or scale.

4. Encoding rules

Numeric values are encoded in the smallest representation that can hold them without loss. Integers are encoded as variable-length quantities using the scheme described in Section 4.2. Floating point values are encoded in IEEE 754 binary32 unless the channel definition specifies binary64. Text is encoded in UTF-8 without a byte order mark, and implementations must reject strings containing unpaired surrogates or overlong encodings.

5. Error handling

A receiver that detects an error must not attempt to resynchronise by scanning for the next header within the same buffer; it must discard the remainder of the frame and wait for the next one. This rule exists because resynchronisation has historically caused receivers to interpret payload bytes as headers and to report measurements that were never taken. Implementations that log discarded frames should record the reason for the discard and the offset at which the frame began.

6. Registration

Requests for channel identifiers are submitted to the registrar in writing and are reviewed twice a year. The registrar maintains a public list of assigned identifiers, together with the measurement type, unit and scale associated with each one. Identifiers that have not been observed in traffic for a period of five years may be reclaimed after a notice period of twelve months.

7. Conformance

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
